what_its_for: Sarilumab is used to treat moderate to severe rheumatoid arthritis (RA) in adults when other medicines have not worked well enough. It helps reduce joint pain, swelling, and stiffness by blocking a protein in your body called IL-6, which causes inflammation.
how_to_take: Sarilumab is given as an injection under your skin (subcutaneous injection), usually in your stomach area (abdomen), thigh, or upper arm. It comes in a pre-filled syringe or a pre-filled pen. Your doctor or nurse will show you how to inject it properly. Always rotate the injection site each time and never inject into skin that is red, bruised, tender, or hard.
dosing: The usual dose is 200 mg injected under the skin once every 2 weeks. Your doctor may lower your dose to 150 mg every 2 weeks if you have certain side effects, such as low white blood cell counts or liver enzyme changes. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, inject it as soon as you remember — but only if your next scheduled dose is more than 7 days away. If your next dose is within 7 days, skip the missed dose and continue on your regular schedule. Do not inject two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store sarilumab in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Keep it in its original carton to protect it from light. Do not freeze it, and do not use it if it has been frozen. If needed, you may store it at room temperature (up to 77°F / 25°C) for up to 14 days — but once taken out of the refrigerator, do not put it back. Throw it away after 14 days at room temperature or by the expiration date, whichever comes first.
what_to_avoid: Avoid receiving live vaccines (such as measles, mumps, rubella, chickenpox, or nasal flu vaccine) while taking sarilumab, as this could cause serious infections. Avoid close contact with people who are sick, especially those with infections. Do not start sarilumab if you currently have an active infection. Avoid sharing your pen or syringe with others.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you have: signs of infection such as fever, chills, cough, or painful urination; unusual tiredness or weakness; stomach pain, nausea, or yellowing of your skin or eyes (signs of liver problems); signs of a serious allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing; any new or worsening symptoms. Also tell your doctor if you have ever had tuberculosis (TB) or have been exposed to TB.
when_it_works: Some people begin to feel improvement in joint pain and swelling within a few weeks, but it may take 3 to 6 months to feel the full benefit. Keep taking your medication even if you do not notice immediate changes.
special_populations: Pregnant or breastfeeding women should talk to their doctor before using sarilumab, as it may harm an unborn baby or pass into breast milk. Women who can become pregnant should use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 3 months after the last dose. Sarilumab has not been approved for use in children. Older adults (65 years and older) may have a higher risk of infections and should be monitored closely. Tell your doctor about all your medical conditions, including liver or kidney problems, before starting this medicine.
